\section{Introduction}

Feature selection is a critical step in machine learning workflows, particularly when dealing with high-dimensional datasets. By reducing the number of features, this process enhances model interpretability, accelerates training times, and improves predictive accuracy. Consequently, feature selection has become a widely adopted technique across various domains.

Existing methods for feature selection can be broadly categorized into three types: filter, wrapper, and embedded approaches. Filter methods rely on statistical metrics to evaluate feature relevance, such as correlation coefficients or mutual information. Wrapper methods, in contrast, assess feature subsets based on the performance of a specific machine learning model. Embedded methods integrate feature selection directly into the model training process. While filter methods are computationally efficient, they often overlook feature interactions. Wrapper methods, though more accurate, suffer from high computational costs due to the need to train models for each candidate subset. Embedded methods offer a balance between accuracy and efficiency but are limited to specific algorithms.

In this study, we propose a new wrapper-based feature selection method that utilizes a genetic algorithm to identify the optimal feature subset. Our approach defines a fitness function based on the performance of a machine learning model trained on the selected features. We evaluate our method on both synthetic and real-world datasets and compare it with other feature selection techniques. Additionally, we analyze the computational complexity of our algorithm.
